segments.narration: A Roman hill is made of 53 million broken jars. Thirty-five metres high, nearly a kilometre around. All of it thrown away.
Every jar carried olive oil from southern Spain to feed the city. Around six billion litres. At the peak, 130,000 jars a year.
Rome recycled almost everything. Broken pottery normally went back into concrete. So why smash these and carry the pieces uphill?
Oil-soaked clay wrecks concrete, and these jars broke into curved slabs too big to crush. Dumping them was simply cheaper.
So Rome engineered its dump. Stepped terraces, retaining walls of whole jars, lime for the stink. Painted labels on the pots still record every weight and inspector.

verdicts.claim: Monte Testaccio in Rome is an artificial mound of broken pottery about 35 metres high and nearly 1 kilometre in circumference, containing an estimated 53 million amphorae.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The amphorae were mostly Dressel 20 vessels from Baetica in southern Spain carrying olive oil, around 6 billion litres in total, with up to 130,000 amphorae deposited a year at the late-2nd-century AD peak.
verdicts.note: 89% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 4 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Broken Roman pottery was normally reused, including as aggregate in concrete and as landfill.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia's explanation for the dump turns on Dressel 20 sherds being hard to crush 'into small pieces for reuse in concrete or landfill', which states reuse as the norm these pots failed to meet.

verdicts.claim: Dressel 20 fragments were large and curved and hard to crush small enough for reuse, and residual oil reacting with lime would have weakened concrete, so discarding them was cheaper.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives both reasons - large curved fragments hard to crush, making disposal cheaper, and residual oil reacting with lime to form soap and weaken concrete - as the likely explanation; the Madain Project repeats both. The narration states them as the explanation, which is how both sources frame them, and the article notes it is unclear why only oil containers were used.

verdicts.claim: The mound was engineered in stepped terraces with retaining walls of nearly intact amphorae, lime was sprinkled over the shards probably to mask the smell of rancid oil, and painted tituli picti on the vessels record the oil's weight, the weighers' names and the district of origin.
